en: The *Vimala-vinaya-vaipulya-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great [assembly].
The assembly consisted of eight thousand bhikṣus and twelve thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the devas of the desire and form realms and the sons of the gods from the Pure Abodes.
At that time, the World-Honored One, respectfully surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of followers, expounded the Dharma.
At that time, there was a son of heaven named Silent Subduing Sound who came and sat in the assembly.

Then, the son of heaven Silent Subduing Sound rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"In what place does this Mañjuśrī reside?"
"Now this great assembly thirsts with longing to see this virtuous man and to hear the Dharma from him.
Having been asked thus, the Buddha then addressed the devaputra Śāntavinītaruta:

"To the east, beyond ten thousand buddha-fields from here, there is a buddha-field named Ratnādhipati. Therein dwells a Buddha, titled Ratnalakṣaṇa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides and teaches the Dharma."
“Mañjuśrī resides in that land, turning the wheel of Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Then, that son of heaven addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I pray that you manifest a sign to cause Mañjuśrī to come to this land.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
If one were to hear the Dharma from all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it would not be equal to hearing the Dharma from Mañjuśrī.
Except for the Tathāgata, there is no one who excels him in preaching the Dharma.
When Mañjuśrī expounds the Dharma, all the palaces of Māra are completely eclipsed in darkness; he is able to subdue all the Māras, causing them to abandon overweening pride and extinguish it.

If there are those who have not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta, may they resolve to do so; for those who have already resolved, may they abide in non-retrogression. May those who can be gathered be gathered, and those who must be relinquished be relinquished, in accordance with the Tathāgata’s wish that the True Dharma endure for a long time.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having known the mind of the Devaputra Silent Subduing Sound, emitted light from the treasury of his white tuft of hair, which universally illuminated this Buddha-world and, proceeding eastward beyond ten thousand Buddha-lands, shone throughout that Treasure-Lord World.
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the world-system Ratnapati, having seen this light, addressed the Buddha Ratnalakṣaṇa, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What kind of radiant sign is this, such that this light shines everywhere throughout this realm?”
Having been asked thus, the Buddha Ratnākara addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
To the west, ten thousand buddha-fields from here, there is a land named Sahā. Therein dwells a Buddha, titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma."
"That Tathāgata has emitted a single ray of light from the tuft between his eyebrows; this light has penetrated ten thousand Buddha-fields to illuminate this world-system.
These bodhisattvas addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"For what cause and condition has that Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, emitted a single ray of light from the tuft between his eyebrows?"
The Buddha then replied:

"In the land of that Tathāgata Śākyamuni, there are immeasurable thousands of billions of bodhisattvas who have all assembled, along with Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, and the entire fourfold assembly; they wish to see the youth Mañjuśrī and hear the Dharma from him."
"For this reason, I request that Śākyamuni Tathāgata release a single ray of light from the tuft of hair between his brows.
At that time, Ratnaketu Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
"You should now go to the Sahā world."
“Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, desires to see you and the great assembly, and they desire to hear and see the Dharma.
Mañjuśrī addressed that Blessed One:
“I too now recognize such an auspicious omen of light.”

At that time, Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King, together with ten thousand bodhisattvas, prostrated his head at the feet of the Buddha Ratnaketu. Then, in the time it takes a strong man to flex and extend his arm, he and the ten thousand bodhisattvas vanished from the realm of Ratnāvatī and arrived in the Sahā world.

Abiding in mid-air without manifesting a physical form, they rained down various kinds of flowers as offerings to the Tathāgata and the great assembly, piling up to the knees—multicolored, exquisite, and pleasing to the senses with their fragrance and hue.
When the entire great assembly saw this rain of flowers falling, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What is this preceding sign that causes such a heavy rain of these flowers?
The Buddha said:

“Good sons! This Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King, has come to this Sahā world accompanied by ten thousand bodhisattvas; he dwells in mid-air without manifesting his form, raining down flowers as an offering to me.”
Then the great assembly, with one voice, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"We wish to see Mañjuśrī, the Prince of the Dharma, and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that we may behold their forms."

Then Mañjuśrī and ten thousand bodhisattvas descended from the sky; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and completed circumambulating him to the right, each manifested a seat through their supernormal powers and sat down to one side.
Then the devaputra Silent Subduing Sound addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray that you will question Mañjuśrī, the Son of the Dharma King, regarding the discourse on establishing [the teachings], which the assembly desires to hear."
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"Now you should ask Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King, whatever you doubt.
Then the devaputra Silent Subduing Sound asked Mañjuśrī:
“How does that Buddha Ratnaketu teach the Dharma in his buddha-field,
such that you take delight in it? Mañjuśrī replied,
“O Devaputra!...”

He does not give rise to desire nor extinguish desire; he does not give rise to hatred nor extinguish hatred; he does not give rise to delusion nor extinguish delusion; he does not give rise to afflictions nor extinguish afflictions.
"Why is this? Because dharmas that are unarisen can never undergo cessation.
The devaputra asked:
“Mañjuśrī, how is it that the sentient beings in that land neither give rise to the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, nor do they extinguish them?
He replied:
"No, O Son of Heaven! The Son of Heaven asked:
"What is it that those Buddhas teach for the sake of severing?
He replied,
"They expound the Dharma for the sake of neither arising nor ceasing."
Why is this? Because in that buddha-field, there is no knowledge of severance, nor is there cultivation or realization.
Those sentient beings value the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and do not value conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The devaputra asked,
“Mañjuśrī, what is called the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya)?”
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra!

That which neither abides in arising nor abides in cessation has no characteristic of location, yet is not without the characteristic of location; it is neither with characteristics nor without characteristics, neither with characteristics nor empty space. Its formal characteristics (rūpalakṣaṇa) are neither characterizable nor uncharacterizable; it is neither exhaustible nor capable of being exhausted, and being inexhaustible, there is nothing that can exhaust it. This is what is called the Ultimate Truth (paramārthasatya)."
"O Son of Heaven!

The ultimate meaning (paramārtha) is neither mind nor the continuity of mind; it is not a phrase of verbal expression; it is without 'this' or 'that,' nor is there anything intermediate between them. To speak thus is called the First Noble Truth (paramārthasatya)."
"O Son of Heaven!
Furthermore, that which is called 'meaning' is ungraspable and devoid of the activity of words; this is termed the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya). Why is this so?"
The Buddha has said that all sounds whatsoever are false.
The devaputra said, “Mañjuśrī?”
"Can that which the Tathāgata has spoken be false? "O Devaputra!
That which the Tathāgata has spoken is neither real nor false."

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has no dualistic characteristics; his mind abides nowhere and is beyond verbal expression; he is neither a conditioned phenomenon nor an unconditioned phenomenon; he speaks neither of reality nor of unreality, for he is free from dualistic characteristics.
"Son of Heaven!
What do you think?
If a person created by a Tathāgata were to say something, would it be real or false?"
He replied:
"It is neither real nor false. Why is this so?"
"Because the person manifested by the Tathāgata has no reality.
Mañjuśrī said: "So it is, so it is."
"O Son of Heaven!
All dharmas are without accomplishment; what the Tathāgata has spoken is neither real nor false, and is therefore called 'non-dual'.
The Son of Heaven said:
“Mañjuśrī, how does the Tathāgata teach the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya)? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
There is no one capable of expounding the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Why is this?
"This is beyond verbal expression, and there is no one capable of speaking it.
When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred bhikṣus were no longer grasping at any phenomena; their outflows were exhausted, and their minds attained liberation.
Two hundred devaputras attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti).
At that time, the Devaputra Silent Subduing Sound asked Mañjuśrī,
“The ultimate truth is extremely difficult to understand.
Mañjuśrī replied:
"So it is, so it is, O Devaputra!
The ultimate truth is indeed difficult to understand; it is truly difficult to understand for those who do not practice correctly."
The devaputra asked:
“Mañjuśrī, in what way is a bodhisattva said to be practicing correctly?”
Mañjuśrī said: “If one does not say:
‘I know this, I abandon this, I cultivate this, I realize this.’”
Why is this? If there is a sign, it is craving, it is attachment, it is conceptual proliferation.
If someone were to say:
"To say, 'This should be known, this should be abandoned, this should be cultivated,
and this should be realized,' is not what is called correct practice.
The Devaputra asked:
“Mañjuśrī! What is the correct practice of a bodhisattva? “O Devaputra!”
Just as suchness and so forth, the dharma-realm and so forth, and the five heinous crimes and so forth are equal, so too are all views equal to the dharma-realm and so forth.
Just as the dharmas of ordinary beings are equal, the dharmas of those in training and the dharmas of those beyond training are likewise equal.
Just as the Dharma of the śrāvakas is equal, so too are the Dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the Dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and the Buddha-Dharmas equal.
Just as the Dharma of saṃsāra is equal, so too are the Dharmas of nirvāṇa, the afflictions, and disputes equal.
The devaputra asked:
“Mañjuśrī, how is it that even afflictions such as contention and dispute are equal?”
Mañjuśrī said: "They are equal because they are empty;
they are equal because they are signless; they are equal because they are wishless. Why is this?"
"Because emptiness is without differentiation,
O Devaputra!
Just as the space within a precious vessel and the space within an earthenware vessel are equal and without difference, being neither manifold nor dualistic."
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!
Just as the emptiness of afflictions and the emptiness of disputes are without distinction and are non-dual.
The Devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! Does a bodhisattva ever cultivate the noble truths? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! If a bodhisattva does not cultivate the noble truths, how could they possibly preach the Dharma for the śrāvakas?
Furthermore, Devaputra!”
When a bodhisattva cultivates the noble truths, there is contemplation; when a śrāvaka cultivates the noble truths, there is no contemplation.
When a bodhisattva cultivates the noble truths, there is leisure; when a śrāvaka cultivates the noble truths, there is no leisure.
The Bodhisattva cultivates the Noble Truths with conditions, whereas the Śrāvaka cultivates the Noble Truths without conditions.
The Bodhisattva cultivates the Noble Truths and contemplates them correctly, yet does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
When a bodhisattva cultivates the noble truths, they possess skillful means; they do not turn their back on saṃsāra nor do they head toward nirvāṇa.
When a bodhisattva cultivates the contemplation of the noble truths, they contemplate all Buddha-dharmas.
"O Son of Heaven!

It is like a person who abandons a great caravan leader and, alone and without a companion, wishes to cross a vast wilderness; his heart is filled with extreme terror, and he does not dare to turn back."
In this way, O Devaputra!
It is the same with the śrāvaka: terrified of birth and death, they do not return to the world; abandoning all sentient beings, they do not return to the cycle of birth and death.
Failing to contemplate the Buddha-dharma and its skillful means, they practice the Noble Truths alone and without a second.
"O Devaputra!
It is like a great caravan leader who has many followers, vast wealth, and abundant provisions, seeking to cross a desolate wilderness for the sake of great profit."

"O Son of Heaven! Thus, the Bodhisattva acts as a great leader with many companions and a vast retinue; he accomplishes the great benefit of the Dharma and amasses a great store of Dharma-provisions. He is fully endowed with the six pāramitās and perfects the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). Universally observing all sentient beings as conditions, he contemplates the revolving flow of birth and death while correctly contemplating the Buddha-Dharma. Traveling from one buddha-field to another, he is endowed with skillful means (*upāya*) and cultivates the Noble Truths."
"O Devaputra!
Just as when a thin and porous object is perfumed with the fragrance of the Campaka, Kumuda, or Pāṭala flowers, the scent quickly emerges;
so it is, O Devaputra!"
The Śrāvakas cultivate the Truths with such rapidity that they enter Nirvāṇa before their aspirations are fulfilled.

They likewise do not emerge from the fragrance of the Buddha’s virtues—his ethical discipline, learning, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—and furthermore, they are unable to sever the habitual tendencies of affliction.
"O Son of Heaven!

It is like a garment from Kāśī: if it is perfumed with celestial jewels and agallochum incense for hundreds or thousands of years, it will possess a pure and exquisite fragrance that is revered by both humans and devas."
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
For hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, the Bodhisattva constantly cultivates the Noble Truths, not entering nirvana midway because he desires to fulfill his original vow.

He emits the fragrance of the Buddha’s precepts, hearing, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; he is able to sever the habitual tendencies of the fetters, and is thus revered by all humans, devas, asuras, gandharvas, and others.
The devaputra Śāntadamasvara again asked Mañjuśrī:
"What are the śrāvaka assemblies in that buddha-field of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnākara like? How do they delight in it?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra!
In that land, the śrāvakas do not abide in faith, they do not teach others to have faith, and they do not protect the dharma-dhātu."
The eight persons have transcended the eightfold wrong paths; it is not the srotāpanna who has transcended the evil realms;
it is not the sakṛdāgāmin who goes and returns to teach and transform all sentient beings; it is not the anāgāmin because all dharmas are without coming or going;
it is not the arhat who receives offerings from all the three thousandfold worlds; nor is it the śrāvaka who is able [to do so].

They uphold all the teachings spoken by all Buddhas; they do not sever desire yet are not tormented by desire, they do not sever hatred yet are not tormented by hatred, and they do not sever delusion yet are not tormented by delusion. Regarding all phenomena, they are free from all darkness and obscurations;
they do not sever the afflictions, but diligently practice vigor to sever the afflictions of all sentient beings.
Afflictions are forever without arising; transcending all modes of birth, they manifest according to the mind's desire.
They are devoid of the marks of self, person, or sentient being, yet they teach and transform sentient beings without grasping or giving. All such sentient beings are pure fields of merit.

One cultivates right mindfulness without thought or recollection; one cultivates right abandonment without arising or ceasing; one gives rise to the bases of supernormal power by distancing oneself from body and mind; one cultivates the faculties by knowing the faculties of all sentient beings and reaching the further shore; one cultivates the powers by crushing all fetters; one cultivates awakening by universal knowledge; one attains the unconditioned without realizing [a limited] path; one cultivates concentration by reaching the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); one cultivates wisdom by reaching the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); one gives rise to illumination by exhausting ignorance; and one realizes liberation through non-dual practice.

With the fleshly eye, one sees all sentient beings, all Buddha-lands, and all Buddhas; with the divine eye, one sees all sentient beings dying here and being born there; with the wisdom eye, one perceives that the birth and death of all sentient beings involve neither coming nor going; with the Dharma eye, one sees the equality of all phenomena; and with the Buddha eye, one clearly perceives all Buddha-realms.
With the divine ear, they hear all Buddha-dharmas and are able to receive and uphold them.
With a single mind, they can know the mental activities of all sentient beings and fully know their past lives throughout the limits of kalpas.

Possessing hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are able to traverse immeasurable Buddha-fields. Their afflictions (*kleśa*) are entirely exhausted, yet they do not realize liberation; though they may be seen, they are not physical bodies (*rūpakāya*).

Though they possess speech, it is devoid of literal characters; though they possess thought, their minds are unmoving. Their form and color are sublime and wondrous, adorned with all the marks of excellence; their garlands of merit and majesty are difficult to withstand. Their fame is lofty and far-reaching, and pure precepts serve as their unguent. They are unsullied by worldly dharmas and untainted by afflictions. Free from coarse or evil speech, they sport in supernormal powers; their learning is vast and increasing, and their eloquence (*pratibhāna*) roars like a thunderclap. They are skilled in transformations, subduing the darkness [of ignorance] with the bright illumination of great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*). Their discourse is unhindered and their dharanis are ultimate; they are always protected and remembered by all Buddhas.

The mindfulness of the śrāvakas is constant and focused; however, the mindfulness regarding the path to bodhi is like the ocean. Its concentration is like Mount Sumeru, its forbearance like the great earth, and its courageous subduing of Māra is like that of Śakra. It cannot be disparaged by anyone, being as tranquil as Brahmā; it is peerless and equal to nothing, pervading all things like empty space.
"O Son of Heaven!
Such are the śrāvakas in that Buddha-field of Ratnākara;
their merits exceed even this."

When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred bhikṣus, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, and five thousand devaputras who were oriented toward the wisdom of śrāvakas spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!...”
"We vow to become the assembly of śrāvakas for that Tathāgata Ratnākṣa.
Mañjuśrī said, "Good sons!..."
The mind of a śrāvaka cannot give rise to rebirth in that land.
You all should resolve to attain the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment; only then can you be born in that land.
All those who are born there have resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, these beings immediately resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path, and the Tathāgata prophesied that they would all be born in that land.
Then, the Devaputra Śāntavinayasvara asked Mañjuśrī,
“What is called the *vinaya* of a bodhisattva?”
"What is called the śrāvaka-vinaya?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!..."
The Vinaya of the three realms that arises from fear is the Vinaya of the śrāvakas;
the Vinaya of the three realms that arises from accepting immeasurable birth and death with the desire to transform all sentient beings is the Vinaya of the bodhisattvas.
The Vinaya that adorns merit through disparaging others is the Vinaya of the Śrāvakas;
the Vinaya that adorns merit by personally accumulating it is the Vinaya of the Bodhisattvas.
To sever all fetters of affliction for oneself is the *vinaya* of the śrāvaka;
to desire to sever the afflictions of all sentient beings is the *vinaya* of the bodhisattva.
Not keeping in mind the maturation of all sentient beings and all Buddha-dharmas is the *vinaya* of the śrāvaka;
keeping in mind the desire to mature all sentient beings and all Buddha-dharmas is the *vinaya* of the bodhisattva.
That which is not known by all the devas is the *vinaya* of the śrāvakas;
that which is known by all the devas throughout the entire trichiliocosm is the *vinaya* of the bodhisattvas.
The relinquishing of all Māras is the *vinaya* of the śrāvakas;
the wailing and lamentation of all Māras throughout the trichiliocosm, and the arising of feelings of enmity and the desire to subjugate among all the Māras, is the *vinaya* of the bodhisattvas.
To illuminate only [oneself] is the *vinaya* of the śrāvakas;
to universally desire to illuminate all worlds and to desire to illuminate and accomplish all Buddha-dharmas is the *vinaya* of the bodhisattvas.
Observing one's own mind is the *vinaya* of the śrāvakas;
observing all Buddha-dharmas is the *vinaya* of the bodhisattvas.
Gradual *vinaya* is the *vinaya* of the śrāvakas;
To know all in a single thought is the *vinaya* of a bodhisattva;
to sever the lineage of the Triple Gem is the *vinaya* of a śrāvaka;
to uphold the lineage of the Triple Gem is the *vinaya* of a bodhisattva.
That which is like a broken earthenware vessel that cannot be repaired is the *vinaya* of the śrāvakas;
that which is like a gold or silver vessel that can be mended when broken is the *vinaya* of the bodhisattvas.
The absence of skillful means is the *vinaya* of the śrāvaka;
the accomplishment of skillful means is the *vinaya* of the bodhisattva.
The absence of the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses is the *vinaya* of the śrāvaka.
The accomplishment of the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses is the *vinaya* of the bodhisattva;
the small fruits and fruit trees are the *vinaya* of the śrāvaka;
and the pleasure groves, halls, pavilions, and the joy of the Dharma are the *vinaya* of the bodhisattva.
The absence of the six pāramitās and the four means of integration is the vinaya of the śrāvaka;
the presence of the six pāramitās and the possession of the four means of integration is the vinaya of the bodhisattva.
Not severing any habitual tendencies is the *vinaya* of the śrāvaka;
extinguishing all habitual tendencies is the *vinaya* of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!

Briefly stated, that which is comprised of the finite, possessing limited qualities of the Dharma, and limited precepts, learning, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, is the Vinaya of the Śrāvakas;

that which is comprised of the immeasurable and immeasurable, possessing immeasurable qualities, immeasurable precepts, learning, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, is the Vinaya of the Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
"You have eloquently explained this *vinaya* of the bodhisattvas. Mañjuśrī,
listen as I briefly explain how to fulfill your meaning."
Mañjuśrī! It is like two people: one praises the great ocean, while the other extols a cow’s footprint. Mañjuśrī!
"What do you think?
Could this person praise all the merit contained within these ox tracks?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“World-Honored One!
The great ocean is immeasurable, while a cow’s footprint is extremely small; what should be praised?
The Buddha said:
"It is so. One should know that the *vinaya* of the śrāvakas is like a cow's footprint—small, devoid of merit, and not worthy of praise.
It is the same with those who belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle."
Mañjuśrī, what do you think?
Would that second person be able to praise the merits of the great ocean?
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One!
This great ocean possesses immeasurable merits and immeasurable qualities worthy of praise.”
The Buddha said:
"You should know that the *vinaya* of the bodhisattvas is also like this.
It is, for example, like the great ocean, with its immeasurable merits and immeasurable qualities worthy of praise."
"You should know that the Mahāyāna is also like this.
When this Dharma was being taught, twelve thousand devaputras resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!"
"We, too, shall practice and study this Bodhisattva-vinaya to discipline all immeasurable sentient beings.
Then, the Devaputra Silent Subduing Sound asked Mañjuśrī,
"What kind of vinaya are you now practicing and studying?"
"Is it the Vinaya of the Śrāvakas, the Vinaya of the Pratyekabuddhas,
or the Vinaya of the Bodhisattvas? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Devaputra!"
"What do you think?
Is there any great ocean that does not receive the various waters?
The devaputra replied:
“Mañjuśrī! There is no great ocean that does not receive the various waters. Mañjuśrī said:
“Thus it is, O Devaputra!

The *vinaya* of the bodhisattva is like the great ocean; there is no *vinaya* that it does not receive, namely: the *vinaya* of the śrāvaka, the *vinaya* of the pratyekabuddha, the *vinaya* of the bodhisattva, and all *vinayas*.
The devaputra said:
"Mañjuśrī! Regarding that which is called *vinaya*, what is the meaning of *vinaya*?"
Mañjuśrī said: “Devaputra!
‘Vinaya, vinaya’ means the subduing of afflictions.”
"It is called Vinaya because it brings about the knowledge of afflictions.
The Devaputra said: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"How should one cultivate the subduing of afflictions?
How does one know afflictions? Mañjuśrī replied:

Whether through one's own conceptualization, another's conceptualization, or the improper mindfulness of both one's own and another's conceptualization; whether through the self-perception and other-perception that are inverted and unreal; or when bound by various views with ignorance as the primary cause—in such cases, afflictions are able to arise.

If one does not falsely imagine based on oneself, does not falsely imagine based on another, and does not falsely imagine based on both self and other; if one maintains focused and correct mindfulness without thoughts of self or other; if one cuts off perversions and does not dwell in various views; and if one eliminates ignorance and does not engage in dualistic conduct—then afflictions will not arise. That afflictions do not arise is ultimate *vinaya*.
"O Son of Heaven! This is called ultimate discipline (*atyanta-vinaya*).

If, through noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*), one knows that afflictions (*kleśa*) are false, deceptive, and non-existent; that they have no master, no self, and no point of attachment; that they have no place of origin or destination; that they have no direction and are not without direction; that they cannot be apprehended as internal, external, or intermediate; and that they are without accumulation, without hoarding, without form, and without color—this is what is meant by knowing afflictions."
"O Son of Heaven!
Just as a person who knows the nature of a venomous snake can neutralize its poison,
so too, if one knows the nature of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), one can pacify the afflictions (*kleśa*)."
The devaputra asked:
"What is meant by the 'nature of afflictions'? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the seed of affliction (*kleśa*).

If one does not construct conceptually, then [affliction] does not arise; if it does not arise, it is not an affliction. If there is no affliction, there is no dwelling place (*layana*); if there is no dwelling place, there is nothing to be burned and nothing in which to abide. To have no abode is called ultimate discipline (*atyanta-vinaya*).”
"This is what is called knowing the nature of afflictions.
The devaputra asked:
"How is this so, Mañjuśrī?"
"Is this the subduing of afflictions?
Is it real or unreal?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra!
It is like a person who, in a dream, is bitten by a venomous snake; because of the pain, he takes an antidote, whereby the snake's venom is eliminated and the pain is cured.”
"Son of Heaven!
What do you think?
Is that person who was bitten by the snake real or unreal?"
The devaputra replied:
"Mañjuśrī! This is unreal."
"Since there is no reality, what poison should be removed?
Mañjuśrī replied, "The venomous snake is unreal, and its removal is likewise unreal; one should understand it in this way."
The various noble Vinayas are also like this,
O Devaputra!
You have spoken these words:
"What is this 'subduing of afflictions'?
Is it real or is it unreal?
"O Devaputra! [The Buddha replied:]
If there is no self, there are no afflictions;
if the self were real, afflictions would also be real.
Within this, neither a self nor a non-self, nor afflictions nor the absence of afflictions, can be apprehended at all.
If it is thus, how should one discipline them?
For what reason,
O Devaputra?
All phenomena are quiescent because they are unarisen.
All phenomena are quiescent because they cannot be grasped.
All phenomena are quiescent because they lack form and characteristics.
All phenomena are exhausted because they possess nothingness.
All phenomena are inexhaustible because they are unarisen.
All phenomena are unarisen because they possess nothingness.
All phenomena are without cessation, because they lack any solid reality.
All phenomena are without action, because there is no agent.
All phenomena are without action, because there is no self.
All phenomena are without self, because they have no master.
All phenomena are without master, because they are like space.
All phenomena have no coming, because they have no intrinsic substance.
All phenomena have no going, because they are without limits.
All phenomena have no abiding, because they have no place of abiding.
All phenomena have no abiding, because they are without arising or ceasing.
"O Son of Heaven! All dharmas are unconditioned because they are without outflows.
All dharmas are without giving, because they are ultimately tamed."
The devaputra Śāntavinītaghoṣa again asked Mañjuśrī:
“What serves as the gateway to all dharmas?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"The door of improper cultivation increases birth and death;
the door of proper cultivation attains nirvana.
Through the door of proper cultivation, one gains mastery."
The gate of improper cultivation is so called because one does not attain mastery;
the gate of doubt and confusion is so called because it is obscured by darkness;
the gate of thorough understanding is so called because it is free from the obscuration of darkness.
The gate of conceptual proliferation increases afflictions;
the gate of non-conceptual proliferation is free from afflictions.
The gate of consciousness possesses fetters and latent tendencies.
The gate of non-cognition, because there are no fetters or afflictions;
the gate of awakening, because of manifold activities;
the gate of tranquility, because all things are utterly still.
The gate of views increases arrogance;
the gate of emptiness extinguishes arrogance.
The gate of evil associates gives rise to all unwholesome dharmas.
The gate of spiritual friends is so called because it gives rise to all wholesome dharmas;
the gate of wrong views is so called because it gives rise to the root of all suffering;
the gate of right views is so called because it gives rise to the root of all goodness.
The gate of stinginess leads to poverty;
the gate of giving leads to great wealth and estates.
The gate of violating the precepts leads to the various evil realms.
The gate of upholding the precepts is because it is the source of all wholesome states;
the gate of contention is because it obstructs all dharmas;
the gate of patience is because it increases the superior dharmas.
The gate of indolence causes the mind to be defiled;
the gate of diligence leaves the mind undefiled.
The gate of applied and sustained thought involves much distraction and clamor.
The gate of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is because the mind is focused on a single point.
The gate of lacking wisdom is like that of a foolish sheep;
the gate of wisdom is because of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).
The gate of loving-kindness, because it does not obstruct wisdom;
the gate of compassion, because it is upright and free from hypocrisy;
the gate of sympathetic joy, because it gathers the treasure of the Dharma.
The gate of relinquishment, because it is free from love and hatred;
the gate of right mindfulness, because one does not lose the original roots of goodness;
the gate of severance, because one cultivates correct practice.
The gateway of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), because the body and mind are light;
the gateway of the faculties (*indriya*), because faith is foremost;
the gateway of the powers (*bala*), because it subdues all afflictions (*kleśa*).
The gate of awakening, because it accords with the awakening to all phenomena;
the gate of the Eightfold Noble Path, because it transcends all non-paths.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
The gateway of the bodhicitta, because it is the source of all Buddha-dharmas;
the gateway that encompasses all dharmas, because it attains mastery over all dharmas;
the gateway that gathers in sentient beings;
Because of expounding the Dharma;
because of the gateways of skillful means;
and because of what is possible and what is impossible.
The gate of wisdom (prajñā) is for reaching the further shore of the mental activities of all sentient beings;
the gate of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) is for the sake of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna);
the gate of the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍ-abhijñā) is for the sake of the light of wisdom.
"The gate of the patience of the gift of Dharma is because one does not follow the wisdom of others.
The Devaputra asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is the gateway to the dharma-realm? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Son of Heaven!"
"The universal gate is the gate of the dharma-realm.
The devaputra asked:
"What realm is the dharma-realm?"
Mañjuśrī said: "The realm of all sentient beings is the Dharma-realm.
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! Does the dharma-realm have a limit?
He replied:
“Son of Heaven!
What do you think?
Does space have a limit?”
"No, Mañjuśrī! O Devaputra!"
"Just as space has no limit, so too is the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) without limit.
The devaputra said, "Mañjuśrī!"
"Do you know the dharma-realm?
He replied, "O Devaputra!"
"The Dharma-realm does not know the Dharma-realm.
The devaputra said, "Mañjuśrī!..."
"What dharma do you know that possesses such eloquence?
He replied, "O Devaputra!"
"What do you think?
What dharma does an echo know that it produces sound?
The devaputra replied:
"An echo has no cognition, yet it produces sound; it is through causes and conditions that sound exists.
'In this same way, O Devaputra, a bodhisattva speaks because of sentient beings.'"
The devaputra said:
"Abiding where are you able to speak thus?
He replied:
“Devaputra! Just as that which is spoken by a person created by the Tathāgata while dwelling [in such a state] is so, my dwelling is likewise.
The Devaputra said:
“The person created by the Tathāgata has no place of abiding.
He replied, “Devaputra!
“The Tathāgata transforms beings without abiding anywhere, yet he has something to say; all dharmas likewise do not abide anywhere, yet they have something to say.
The Devaputra said: “Mañjuśrī!
"If all dharmas are without abiding, in what place do you abide to accomplish the Unsurpassed Way?
Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
"I shall dwell in the Avīci hell and attain the Unsurpassed Way.
The devaputra asked:
"In what place does this 'Avīci' dwell?"
He replied,
"It dwells without interval and has no root.
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! Those who dwell in the immediate [states] will inevitably fall into hell.
He replied:
“Devaputra! It is so, it is so.
As the Tathāgata has said, those who commit the five deeds of immediate retribution will certainly fall into hell.”
"O Devaputra!
I too now abide in the five immediate transgressions (ānantarya).
O Devaputra!"
A bodhisattva abides in five kinds of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) and accomplishes the unsurpassed path. What are these five?

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks the unsurpassed path and does not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha in the interim; this is the first immediacy.
"I should rescue and deliver all sentient beings without any slackening in between"—this is the second uninterrupted [practice].
"I shall relinquish all things without any stinginess in between"—this is the third uninterrupted [practice].
To know that all phenomena are unarisen, and in the interim not to dwell together with any views—this is the fourth immediate attainment (*ānantarya*).

Whether through knowing, seeing, or abandoning, one realizes them as equal and perfectly awakened; by means of wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, one awakens to this knowledge, does not arise again in the interim, and will certainly achieve perfect awakening.
"These are the five immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*).
If a bodhisattva abides in these five immediate transgressions, they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The devaputra said:

“Mañjuśrī! Is it possible that an ordinary person, dwelling in the five immediate transgressions, falls into hell, while a bodhisattva, likewise dwelling in these five immediate transgressions, achieves unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment?”
He replied, “There is.
The devaputra said:
"For what reason? He replied,
"O Devaputra!"
All phenomena are empty; because one understands emptiness, it is called attaining bodhi.
All phenomena are signless, wishless, and non-conditioned; they are without arising and without cause, yet arise through dependent origination.
"Awakening is so called because it is a causal condition; therefore, it is named 'awakening to bodhi'.
The Devaputra said: "Mañjuśrī!"
"Who would believe this Dharma?
He replied, "O Devaputra!"
"If even a Buddha-Tathāgata would not yet give rise to faith, how much less so a śrāvaka?
The devaputra asked again:
"Who understands this Dharma?"
He replied,
"One who does not practice the mark of a self.
He asked again:
"Who will believe this Dharma?
He replied,
"Those who do not abide on this shore or the other shore."
The devaputra said:
"If one does not abide in this or that, who would conceive of this dharma?
He replied:
"One who has no recollection or conceptualization regarding any phenomena.
He asked again:
"Who maintains it?"
He replied,
"It is held by one who does not maintain any fetters.
The devaputra asked again:
"To whose hands shall this sutra come?
He replied,
"It shall come into the hands of those who bestow the Dharma upon all sentient beings."
He asked again,
"What is its shape and color?
He replied:
“Devaputra! That is the form of dharmas; it is not the form of the aggregates, elements, or sense bases.
He asked again:
"What is his practice? He replied,
"He practices emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."
He asked again:
"Where does he go? He replied:
“Devaputra!
He shall proceed toward all destinations, reach the mental activities of all sentient beings, and arrive at the state of non-arrival.
The Devaputra asked:
“Mañjuśrī, does a bodhisattva fall back?
He replied:
“Devaputra! It is impossible that a bodhisattva should fall back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The devaputra said:
"Who is it that regresses?
He replied,
"All afflictions regress, and all stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas regress."
He asked again:
"Who is non-retrogressive?
He replied:
"One who possesses samādhi and the like does not regress.
The devaputra said: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is samādhi? He replied,
"It is non-duality and the absence of distinction."
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! If all dharmas have no differentiation, what is it that differentiates?”
He replied: "O Devaputra!
Those who do not know that all dharmas are equal differentiate them into two; they practice dualistic conduct and fall into dualistic conduct."
"If one knows equality, one does not act with differentiation.
If one knows equality, one proceeds toward equality.
The devaputra asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! Is there any bodhisattva who, possessing afflictions, achieves awakening?
He replied:
"It exists.
The Son of Heaven asked again, "Who is it?"
He replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
If a bodhisattva were to sever the fetters and latent tendencies, he would be a śrāvaka."

If a bodhisattva, knowing the afflictions and fetters of all sentient beings, gives rise to an intensification of great compassion and awakens the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, this is bodhi.
The devaputra asked:
"Is it possible for stinginess to become the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)?
He replied:
“There is. He asked, “Who is it?”
He replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
If a bodhisattva does not abandon the mind of enlightenment and gathers in and protects sentient beings, such stinginess is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)."
The devaputra asked again:
"Is there such a thing as the violation of the precepts that is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)? He replied:
“There is. He asked, “Who is it?”
He replied: "Devaputra!
If a bodhisattva greatly benefits all sentient beings while not regarding his own precepts, such a violation of the precepts is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)."
“Mañjuśrī! Is there any bodhisattva who abandons patience that is called the perfection of patience?
He replied:
“There is. He asked, “Who is it?”
He replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
If a bodhisattva relinquishes the prohibitive precepts of non-Buddhists and firmly abides in the Buddha's precepts, this is called the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā)."
“Mañjuśrī! Is it possible for one who is indolent to fulfill the perfection of diligence?
He replied:
“There is. He asked, “Who is it?”
He replied: "Devaputra!
If a bodhisattva gives rise to indolence regarding the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, yet diligently cultivates the unsurpassed right path, this is called the pāramitā of vīrya."
“Mañjuśrī! Is there such a thing as an undetermined mind that is called the dhyānapāramitā?
He replied:
“There is. He asked, “Who is it?”
He replied: "Devaputra!
When a bodhisattva does not give rise to the mind of the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas even within a dream, that is the bodhisattva’s indeterminate mind; this is called the dhyāna-pāramitā."
“Mañjuśrī! Is there such a thing as the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā that is devoid of wisdom?
He replied:
"There is. He asked, "Who is it?"
He replied: "O Devaputra!

It is said that one who lacks wisdom is not a bodhisattva. A bodhisattva does not perform any worldly sorcery, evil incantations, suppressive rites, or rites for inducing madness; rather, they bring suffering to all sentient beings through the Dharma-wisdom [of such arts]. When a bodhisattva achieves and possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), this is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī:
“Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
You have well explained what a bodhisattva should and should not do; Mañjuśrī,
listen as I speak briefly.
Mañjuśrī! Just as a person who is hungry and emaciated would rather endure the suffering of hunger than ever consume food mixed with poison, so it is with the bodhisattva:

they would rather be stingy and greedy, violate the precepts, harbor anger and strife, be indolent, have a distracted mind and false thoughts, or be foolish and lacking wisdom, than dwell in the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, while maintaining right mindfulness in giving, morality, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom.
"Why is this? A bodhisattva should give rise to fear regarding this.
The devaputra asked the Buddha:
“Is it not that a bodhisattva fears the fetters?
The Buddha said,
“One should fear them.”
"O Devaputra!
A bodhisattva should instead give rise to even greater fear regarding the stage of the śrāvaka.
O Devaputra!"
“What do you think?
When a person protects their life, is it out of fear of having their head cut off, or out of fear of having their hands and feet cut off?
The devaputra addressed the Buddha:
"He fears the decapitation, but does not fear his hands and feet. Why is this?
World-Honored One!"
"A person whose hands and feet have been severed is still able to cultivate meritorious deeds; by this cause and condition, they attain rebirth in the heavens.
World-Honored One!
If a person has their head severed and loses their life, they cannot cultivate virtuous conduct."
The Buddha said: "So it is,
O Devaputra!"
A bodhisattva would rather violate the prohibitive precepts than ever abandon the mind of omniscience;
they would rather possess all afflictions as a bodhisattva than ever become a *śrāvaka* arhat who has exhausted all outflows.
The devaputra exclaimed:
"How rare, World-Honored One!
The conduct of these bodhisattvas surpasses that of all other worlds."
“World-Honored One!
For the śrāvakas, to maintain the precepts and apply themselves with diligent vigor is, for the bodhisattvas, to violate the prohibitions and be indolent.
The Buddha said:
"It is so, it is so. It is just as you have said,
O Devaputra!"
Just as the food of a poor man is poison for a wheel-turning monarch,
so it is, O Son of Heaven!
Although a śrāvaka diligently exerts himself to sever all afflictions, he cannot yet bring peace and happiness even to the beings of Jambudvīpa, let alone to all sentient beings.
“O Son of Heaven!
Just as a great caravan leader with vast wealth and fiefdom practices great renunciation and diligent progress, bringing benefit, peace, and nourishment to many;

so too does the Bodhisattva practice great compassion, giving rise to the cultivation of great pity for all sentient beings, diligently nurturing immeasurable beings and enabling them to attain both worldly and world-transcending happiness.”
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The śrāvakas realize unconditioned dharmas, whereas bodhisattvas possess only conditioned dharmas.”
"How is it that a bodhisattva who is conditioned is superior to a śrāvaka who is unconditioned?
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
I shall now provide an analogy so that those who possess wisdom may understand through it. Kāśyapa!
Suppose, for example, there were a person who split a single hair into one hundred parts, and then used one such part of hair to skim all the ghee contained within the four great oceans.
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
Suppose this person were to take a portion of ghee from the four oceans with a single hair-tip and think thus:
"What I have taken is much more than what was in the ocean.
Kāśyapa replied, "No, it is not."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!”
What do you think?
Between these two portions, which is superior?
Which is greater?
"What is most numerous?
What is of the greatest value?
Kāśyapa replied:

"If one were to take even a thousand-billion *yojana*s of it, the remainder would still be superior, greater, more abundant, and of great value; how much more so when taking but a single drop from a portion the size of a hair?"
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!
It is like taking a single strand from a hundred strands of hair and using it to take up a single drop of ghee; such is the unconditioned wisdom possessed by śrāvakas.”

"Kāśyapa, that which is known by the Buddha's wisdom is like the clarified butter filling the four great oceans; so too are the conditioned roots of goodness and merits of a bodhisattva, because they are dedicated toward unconditioned wisdom."
Kāśyapa! It is as if an ant were carrying a single grain, yet it is like the autumn moon when the ripened grain fills the great earth. Kāśyapa!
"What do you think?
Which of these is superior?
"World-Honored One!"
In the autumn moon, the ripened grain fills the great earth; there is immeasurable grain, which serves as sustenance to rescue, nourish, and support immeasurable sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
"A single grain carried by an ant provides no benefit or comfort. Kāśyapa!
The fruit of liberation attained by the śrāvakas is just like that single grain carried by an ant."

Just as autumn crops ripen and fill the great earth, one should know that the roots of goodness and merit of a bodhisattva’s six pāramitās and four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are likewise; they bring to maturity and sustain immeasurable sentient beings, establishing them in worldly happiness, supramundane happiness, and the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa!

Suppose a hundred thousand crystal beads were being carried on a shoulder-pole into a city, and a single priceless lapis lazuli jewel were placed upon a ship; if that ship reached Jambudvīpa in safety, it would rescue and protect all who are poor, destitute, and suffering.
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
Could these hundred thousand loads of crystal entering the city be compared to this single priceless lapis lazuli jewel?
"No, World-Honored One. "Kāśyapa!"
These hundreds of thousands of loads of crystal beads entering the city are a metaphor for the unconditioned merit of the śrāvakas, which is likewise so.

Just as a priceless precious lapis lazuli bead, safely placed upon a ship, reaches Jambudvīpa and brings great peace and happiness to many, so too does the Bodhisattva, by not severing the lineage of the Triple Gem and giving rise to the jewel-mind of omniscience, bring peace and happiness to many.
Then Mahākāśyapa addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"It is unprecedented!
The Tathāgata has spoken excellently."
"All Bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the jewel-like mind of omniscience transcend all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas from the world-system Jewel-Owner who had come with Mañjuśrī, having heard this teaching, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"All verbal expressions are but conceptual proliferation; they are teachings of differentiation and teachings that censure the fetters."
"Bhagavān!
In the buddha-field of Ratnaketu, such discourse does not exist; there is only the teaching of the non-retrogression of bodhisattvas and the teaching of non-differentiation.

It is rare, Bhagavān, that the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is able to endure this suffering, and having realized that all dharmas are without differentiation and without superior, middle, or inferior, he establishes the three vehicles within the single flavor of the dharma-nature."
These bodhisattvas then scattered celestial flowers as an offering over the Buddha and said to Mañjuśrī,
“We should now return to the world of Ratnāvatī.”
Mañjuśrī said: "You may go; you should know that now is the time.
The bodhisattvas replied:
“Will you not go? Mañjuśrī replied,
“O son of good family!”
All worlds are entirely equal; all Buddhas are equal, all dharmas are equal, and all sentient beings are equal.
Abiding therein, what is there for me to do?
The bodhisattvas asked:
"For what reason are all worlds equal, all buddhas equal, all dharmas equal, and all sentient beings equal?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O sons of good family!

All buddha-fields are equal because they are like space; all Buddha-dharmadhātus are equal because they are inconceivable; all dharmas are equal because they are illusory; and all sentient beings are equal because they are without self."
"For this reason, I have spoken thus: 'All worlds are equal, even unto all sentient beings.

At that time, Mañjuśrī manifested his supernormal powers; by means of these powers, he caused the Sahā world-system to be no different from the Ratnāvati world-system, and caused the World-Honored One Śākyamuni to be no different from the Tathāgata Ratnaketu.
Those bodhisattvas each had this thought:
"We have already arrived in the world-system of Ratnākara.
Regarding Śākyamuni Buddha, they conceived the perception that he was Ratnākara Buddha, and they immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Who brought us to this land?
The Buddha said,
“Who took you away?”
The bodhisattvas said,
“The youth Mañjuśrī is taking us away.
The Buddha said:
"He will lead you here.
At that time, Mañjuśrī said to the bodhisattvas:
"Good sons!..."
"Each of you should enter meditative concentration and observe: who brought you here?
Who will take you away?
At that time, the bodhisattvas each entered meditative concentration and observed, each thinking to themselves:
“We did not move from this Sahā world, yet we each thought we had reached the realm of Ratnagarbha.
World-Honored One!
This is truly unprecedented.”
By means of his supernatural powers and the power of samādhi, Mañjuśrī caused us to believe that we had reached the realm of Ratnāvatī, yet this Sahā world remained as it was, unmoved.
“World-Honored One!
May all sentient beings likewise attain such supernatural powers as Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas who had come from the Jewel-Master world:

“Good sons! It is like the space within various vessels—whether vessels of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, quartz, iron, diamond, sandalwood, precious gems, earthenware, or wood. Although the vessels are of many different kinds, the space within them is no different.”

In this way, there is but one dharma-nature, one suchness, and one reality-limit; yet, sentient beings, with their various forms and characteristics, each take up a place of birth. Their own bodies transform into hundreds of thousands of millions of different types of forms and colors, namely: the form of hell-beings, the form of animals, the form of hungry ghosts, the form of devas, the form of humans, the form of śrāvakas, the form of pratyekabuddhas, the form of bodhisattvas, and the form of buddhas.

Because they are equal, form and the other aggregates are equal; because they are like suchness, form and the other aggregates are equal; because they are like emptiness, form and the other aggregates are equal. Good son!
For these reasons, Mañjuśrī says that all worlds are equal, and so on, up to all sentient beings being equal.
"Therefore, it is said: 'I shall not go now.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had thus instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened the bodhisattvas with this Dharma, they prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and before long departed from the assembly to vanish from the Sahā world-system and proceed to the Ratnadhvaja world-system.
At that time, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Receive this sutra, uphold it, read it, recite it, and explain it extensively for others among the great assembly.
The Venerable Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I have received and upheld it,
World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named?”
"How should it be received and upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is named 'The Questions of the Devaputra Śāntadamarasvara'; it is also named 'Pure Vinaya,' and it is also named 'All Buddha-Dharmas.'"

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, the Devaputra Śāntavinītaruta, Mañjuśrī and all the other bodhisattvas, Mahākāśyapa and all the other śrāvakas, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced.
The Sūtra on the Extensive Vinaya of Purification (Vimala-vinaya-vaipulya-sūtra)
